title: Stoic in anger
hook: the jolt, the delay, the other handle

segments.voice: Yesterday: Stoic in grief, with Attalus's saying in mind, honest tears and a memory that turns sweet. Your line was grief, honestly. Did you honor the loss you chose, in one small way? Day six hundred eighty.

The email arrives at 4:52 on a Friday. It's from someone who has been difficult all month, and it's passive-aggressive in a way that's almost artistic. A face goes hot. Fingers start moving. Three sharp sentences are written before the email has even been read to the end. A thumb hovers over send. This year, on the porch, we've met anger more than once: the insult, the other handle, Seneca's long essay on rage. Today we pull it into one tool kit, for the next 4:52 on a Friday. Three moves. Today: Stoic in anger.
screen: `4:52 ON A FRIDAY.` → `THREE SHARP SENTENCES.` → `A THUMB OVER SEND.`

segments.voice: First, the jolt. Seneca, in On Anger, makes a careful distinction. The hot face, the quickened pulse, the first flare: these, he says, aren't yet anger. They're first movements, like the shiver when cold water splashes you, or the way you blink when a hand comes near your eyes. They happen to everyone, even the wise. Feeling the jolt isn't failing. Anger, for Seneca, begins only when the mind agrees: yes, I've been wronged, and they should pay. That agreement is where you still have a choice. Second, the delay. The greatest remedy for anger, Seneca writes, is delay. Not suppression. Just time. Give the first heat a chance to cool, and the judgment underneath a chance to be looked at. An hour. A night. Even a walk around the block. The email will still be there. Third, the other handle. Epictetus, in the Handbook, says everything has two handles, one by which it can be carried and one by which it can't. If your brother wrongs you, don't pick it up by he wronged me; that handle won't carry. Pick it up by he's my brother, we grew up together. With the Friday email: this person is stressed, maybe frightened, maybe having a terrible week. That handle doesn't excuse them. It just lets you carry the thing without dropping it on your foot. Fourth, all three together. Feel the jolt; it's not a crime. Delay the reply; time is medicine. Then find the other handle before you write back. The email sent on Monday is more likely to be shorter, clearer, and something nobody needs to apologize for.
screen: `THE JOLT IS NOT YET ANGER.` · `THE GREATEST REMEDY IS DELAY.` · `PICK IT UP BY THE OTHER HANDLE.` · `JOLT, DELAY, HANDLE, THEN REPLY.` · then, large: `DELAY THE REPLY.`

segments.voice: Recall a recent moment of anger, small enough to look at calmly. Feel, for a second, the jolt it gave you: heat, tightness, speed. Notice that the jolt simply happened. Now imagine pressing pause, letting a full hour go by. Watch the heat lower a little. Then turn the situation around and look for the other handle: what else is true about this person? What might they be carrying? Let that handle settle in your hand. The bell holds the time.
On Anger, Seneca's essay where the first hot jolt is not yet anger, only a first movement, until the mind agrees you've been wronged. Today's word.
Your line: delay the reply. The next time a message makes your face hot, wait at least an hour before you answer it. Day six hundred eighty.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners treat the first flare of anger as involuntary, wait before replying, and then deliberately look for a more charitable way to see the other person.

original.note: Latin, Seneca's On Anger 2: the first movement, the involuntary jolt before anger.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Stoic in anger never gets angry at all.
what it means: the jolt comes to everyone; the Stoic delays, then picks the situation up by the other handle.
what a scholar hears: On Anger 2.2–4 separates involuntary first movements from anger, which needs the mind's assent; 2.29 names delay the greatest remedy; Handbook 43 gives the two handles.
